extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, public administrators, political scientists, civic educators, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for designing and operating public intelligence/research bureaus, conducting representative hearings, and educating the public so that public opinion and administrative decision‑making are better informed and proceduralized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central clearing house / national intelligence bureau
rubrics_metrics.description: A central clearing house (national intelligence bureau) should assemble facts in a way suited to the diplomatic (or administrative) problem up for decision and become a focus of extraordinary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should be open (except for a few diplomatic/military secrets) to scholars; recruit staff from college graduates; link with a 'national university' concept with exchange lecturers and temporary specialist appointments so research and training go together; the bureau provides concrete work for political scientists and students and supports bureaus throughout government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federated state/city/county bureaus and regional coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of organized intelligence work applies to state governments, cities, and counties via federations of bureaus to enable comparison and interchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make accounting systems comparable to avoid duplication; organize regional coordination where legal frontiers differ from effective environments (e.g., metropolitan districts such as New York and surrounding cities); coordination should be of information and research rather than centralized decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation of personnel, data, and criticism to prevent bureaucratic sclerosis
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the intelligence system becoming a dead weight (soft jobs, red tape, excessive paperwork), there must be circulation through government departments, factories, offices, and universities of men, data, and criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation reduces dry rot by promoting self-criticism and reduces personnel per unit of result; warns of anti-patterns such as mountains of paper, excessive forms, endorsements and delays; stresses need for flexible staffing and turnover of temporary specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: aid to representatives and administrators (not mass entertainment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligence bureau is primarily an instrument for the man of action—the representative charged with decision and the worker at his work—and only secondarily a source of general information or a check on the daily press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design outputs and services for those doing public business (accountants, statisticians, secretariats); avoid assuming the general public will or should become expert on every issue through bureau publications; usefulness judged by whether it helps decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize procedural criteria as the continuous role of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside citizens can usually judge procedure (whether relevant facts were duly considered, whether interested groups were heard, whether ballots were honest) but not the technical relevance of facts themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because outsiders cannot typically decide what is relevant, public opinion’s continuous action should focus on principles of procedure; citizens should insist that problems not be brought to them until they have passed through proper procedures that make issues intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert mediation and neutral chair in representative hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative bodies dealing with distant matters should conduct discussion in presence of a chairman or mediator who forces the discussion to deal with analyses supplied by experts; partisans should be confronted by non-involved men who control the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a Socratic-style dialectic carried out by men who have explored the environment as well as the human mind; this untangles partisan rhetoric and allows outsiders to follow proceedings; example: organized hearings in industrial disputes with consulting experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize claims with concrete data and clear definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace vague, emotive claims (e.g., 'well paid' or 'exploited') with concrete tables, defined groups, budgets, and measurable standards (e.g., living wage for groups C, M, X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairmen/mediators should require parties to produce books/data; define terms precisely so emotions are specific to named objects; specificity enables verification, correction by new data, and prevents entanglement of ideas with broad sentimental associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural handling of private or contested data
rubrics_metrics.description: When parties refuse to disclose private books or contest official figures, a chairman may rule that official figures stand and refer technical appeals to the standing committee of federated intelligence bureaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a procedural route for technical disputes and places specialized adjudication with expert bodies rather than the general hearing; it discourages evasions based on 'private' claims that block evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic education oriented to critical source evaluation and models of social systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic education should prepare pupils to examine sources: look for dispatch origin, correspondent’s name, authority for statements, censorship, privacy, and past propaganda; use the case method and comparative history/anthropology to teach how codes shape imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach habits of introspection about imagery, how allegories and dramatization operate, and how to examine sources and reporter track records; equip students with working models of social systems so they can handle unseen environments and the case-method habit of examining evidence and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectical technique: naming and cross‑examination to disentangle emotion and stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: A Socratic/analytic technique that defines words, separates ideas from emotional associations, and names specific objects (e.g., particular worker groups) converts bundled, diffuse feelings into corrigible perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-examination and careful definition make ideas objectified and amenable to correction by data; re-education that emphasizes study of error and scientific victories over superstition helps sustain the discipline of objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence work as the foundation for accumulating social knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Gathering information will be driven by the needs of modern decision-making; as data accumulate, political science can generalize and produce conceptual pictures for schools and for civic education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes current limits (meager instruments, vague concepts); calls for invention and testing of analytic instruments, improved statistics, and systematic research to turn operational information into teachable models and more reliable public intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the appeal to reason: account for time-differentials and crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason advances more slowly than action; in emergencies there is often no time to make each person an expert, so appeals to reason may fail—practical politics must account for the time required for reason to work and the differing pace of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish false crises from real ones; where possible, let longer time horizons control decisions and create footholds for reason; accept that in many urgent decisions quick means (slogans, compromises, force) may be the only feasible option while working on long-term development of reason and institutions.
